passage: Researchers in the Abara laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.
table:
Table 1. Equilibrium and mass-action ratios

| Reaction | Keq | Q in hepatocytes |
|---|---|---|
| glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP | 652 | 6.52 |
| fructose-6-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate | 1.93 | 0.0193 |
| dihydroxyacetone phosphate → glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate | 0.0545 | 0.0545 |

questions.stem: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?

options.B: None; all three are far from equilibrium
options.C: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP

questions.explanation: Q/Keq near 1 indicates near-equilibrium operation. Reaction C has Q closest to Keq, so it is the least likely to be a regulatory step.
questions.trap: Choosing reaction A or B because their Q values are the largest; the test is how close Q is to Keq, which is only true for reaction C (Q/Keq = 1).

questions.stem: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?

options.A: Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
options.B: Measure only product concentration at a single time point
options.C: Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
options.D: Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio

questions.explanation: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated.
questions.trap: Believing a faster rate with more enzyme proves equilibrium; enzyme speeds approach but does not change Keq or show the endpoint was reached.

questions.stem: For reaction B (Keq = 1.93), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
questions.explanation: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(1.93) = -1.7 kJ/mol (literature value -1.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values.
questions.trap: Reversing the sign (+1.7 kJ/mol) by forgetting the minus in ΔG°′ = -RT ln Keq, even though Keq > 1 means ΔG°′ is negative.

options.A: A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell
options.B: A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
options.C: ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
options.D: Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′

questions.explanation: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis.
questions.trap: Assuming a negative ΔG°′ means a fast reaction; thermodynamics gives direction, while the rate depends on activation energy and catalysis.

questions.stem: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?

options.A: Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
options.B: Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
options.C: Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′
options.D: Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis

questions.explanation: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative.
questions.trap: Thinking an enzyme lowers ΔG°′ by raising its concentration; enzymes change rate only and leave ΔG°′ and Keq unchanged.
